Cancellation in C++20 is cooperative, and it has three types. A

The problem it solves is that a thread cannot be killed safely. There is no portable way to stop another thread where it stands, and killing one that holds a mutex or is halfway through a file leaves the program broken. So the standard makes stopping a request the worker agrees to look at, and gives everybody one shared way to express it, instead of the flag each of us used to write.
The mechanism is a shared state with an atomic flag and a list of callbacks. A worker either polls
between units of work, or it waits on
with the overload that takes a token, which ends the wait when the request arrives. A plain
has no such overload, so a worker blocked in it ignores the request and the
destructor waits for it for ever; I measured exactly that, and the program had to be killed.

What it costs is that cooperative means what it says. A worker that never checks is never stopped, a blocking system call is not interrupted, and the destructor blocks until the function returns. It also puts the shutdown order in your hands. Because members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, a
member declared before the data it reads is joined after that data is gone, which is a use-after-free, and AddressSanitizer names it as soon as a test exercises the shutdown. Declare the thread last.

In the robot this is every node's shutdown: a sensor loop that must finish its current frame, a worker pool that should drain what it has accepted, and a logger that must close its file before the process leaves.

The second failure is the one this topic exists for. Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so a
declared first is destroyed last, after every member it reads:

being joined. Take the gate out and the same bug is a race that fires once in a thousand runs, on the customer's machine, in the shutdown path nobody tests.
Read the destruction order out of the declarations.
: the thread is joined last, so it is alive while three members it can reach are destroyed. The stop token does not save it, because the request is part of destroying

is still true when the worker reads.
The fix is the declaration order, and it costs nothing:

The rule is worth stating in one line, because it is the answer to an interview question: a thread member goes last in the class, so it is joined first in the destructor. The same logic explains why the constructor starts the thread in its body rather than in the member initialiser list. Members are constructed in declaration order, so a

initialised in the list of a class that declares it last is started after everything else exists, which is also correct; started in the list of a class that declares it first, it would run while the members below it were still uninitialised. Starting it in the body, after all members are built, works whatever the order and says what it means.
The third failure gives up on ownership altogether. A detached thread has nothing that can stop it, nothing that can wait for it, and no relationship to the lifetime of anything it touches:

blocks.text: main is leaving while the logger still has a second of work

that prints one line and returns, measured at 0.00 seconds of wall clock over three runs, so the output does not depend on how busy the machine is. Had the logger held a lock or been halfway through a file, it would have been stopped there. And had it captured anything by reference from
